title: Hemp vs. Cannabis: Same Plant, Different Law | The Bridge
h1: Hemp vs. Cannabis: Same Plant, Different Law
description: Hemp and cannabis are one plant split by a legal number, and Congress just rewrote how it gets counted. What changes in late 2026, and for New York.
lede: A botanist sees one plant. A lawyer sees two, split by a number, and Congress just rewrote how that number gets counted.
html:
In 1619 the Virginia Assembly passed a law requiring every farmer to grow hemp. The colonies wanted rope, sails and clothing. Four centuries later the same species sits on both sides of a legal wall, and the wall is a number.

One plant, one line

Botanically there is nothing to argue about. New York's Office of Cannabis Management says it flat out: hemp is the same plant as cannabis, in cultivars grown to meet a legal definition. Under federal law, cannabis and its derivatives generally fall into two categories. Hemp is not a controlled substance. Marijuana is. The 2018 farm bill drew the line at 0.3% delta-9 THC.

The gap everybody drove through

That test looked at one molecule. After it passed, the Congressional Research Service recounts, some companies began selling products under 0.3% delta-9 with a total THC above that line. Those products could get people high while legally counting as hemp. Critics called it the THC loophole. Drinks had a special advantage: public health researchers point out that liquid is heavy, so a beverage can hold a high dose and still come in under a percentage limit. Delta-8 products grew up in the same gap, and the FDA says they have not been evaluated or approved for safe use in any context.

The rewrite, and the calendar

In November 2025 Congress changed the definition. As the Congressional Research Service laid it out on October 28, 2026:

  • The 0.3% limit now runs on total THC, not delta-9 alone.
  • Finished hemp-derived products with more than 0.4 milligrams per container of total THC and similar cannabinoids fall out of the definition.
  • Products with cannabinoids the plant can't naturally produce, or that were synthesized outside the plant, are excluded.
  • Industrial hemp grown for stalks, fibers, whole grains, oils and edible greens stays in.

The timing moved. The change was set for November 12, 2026. A later spending law pushed most of it to December 11, 2026, and left only the exclusion for cannabinoids the plant can't naturally produce on the original date. Bills to delay or repeal the changes have been introduced as well, so the calendar may not be finished moving. New York's own explainer adds that the federal limit counts all THC compounds, THCA included.

Cannabis itself isn't standing still either. In April 2026 the Justice Department moved FDA-approved products and state-licensed medical marijuana to Schedule III. As of that same report, all other marijuana, which takes in adult-use, remains in Schedule I. That's why New York still reminds you that you can't consume on federal land.

How New York splits it

New York runs separate tracks. The Department of Agriculture and Markets oversees hemp cultivation and hemp used only for industrial or food purposes. The Office of Cannabis Management regulates hemp used or marketed for its cannabinoid content, such as CBD products, and anyone processing or selling it needs a license. Adult-use cannabis, the classification above 0.3% THC, runs through licensed dispensaries with the universal symbol and lab testing. The state says the federal change does not replace its hemp program, but shoppers may see changes in which hemp-derived products are available.

What it means when you're buying

The word hemp on a package tells you about a legal category. It doesn't tell you what the product will do to you or who checked it. If a product is meant to get you high, ask what you'd ask of anything else: who tested this, and where's the report? At a licensed dispensary the answer is on the label, and the QR code goes to the lab results. Here's how to read it, and you can browse what that looks like in the shop.
